sections.h2: What is property tax like in Bath County, Kentucky?
sections.html:
Bath County covers about 279 square miles on the eastern edge of the Bluegrass, and its property tax is run from a few courthouse offices in Owingsville. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) values land and houses, the sheriff collects the bill, and the county clerk records deeds and receives unpaid bills.

The county was cut from Montgomery County in 1811 and is named for mineral springs once credited with healing powers. Owingsville is the seat and the largest city, with Salt Lick and Sharpsburg the other two cities. A fire set by Union troops destroyed the Owingsville courthouse in 1864, and the county is known for the Kentucky Meat Shower of March 3, 1876, when an unidentified substance fell from the sky. Neighbors are Fleming, Rowan, Menifee, Montgomery, Bourbon and Nicholas counties.

Interstate 64 crosses the county, and Cave Run Lake and the Daniel Boone National Forest take up a large share of its land, which limits where homes can be built.

sections.h2: How big is Bath County, and what do its homes cost?
sections.html:
Bath had 11,591 people in 2010 and 12,750 in 2020, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate of 13,176 adds another 3.4 percent. The 2020 count found 5,445 housing units with 10.4 percent of them vacant, and every resident lived in a rural area.

The Bureau's survey years 2020 through 2024 fill in the market:

  • Price: a middle of the road owned home is worth $129,800.
  • Tenure: owners occupy 74.7 percent of homes, and renters pay a median $659.
  • Income: $56,541 for the median household, with 22.6 percent of residents in poverty.
  • Commuting: 30.0 minutes each way on average, the longest among the four Kentucky counties in these Census tables.
  • Construction: the Bureau logged no building permits for 2025.

With almost no new construction, the houses that change hands are mostly old ones. Age brings deferred repairs, and a PVA record that was never updated can misstate a house in either direction.

sections.h2: Which Bath County office handles which task?
sections.html:
The county site lists each elected office with courthouse contacts. All sit in Owingsville and use separate post office boxes, so address a payment or an appeal to the right desk.

The clerk's site also carries a page of delinquent taxes, handy for checking whether a parcel is listed.

sections.h2: What is the Bath County property tax calendar?
sections.html:
Kentucky fixes value as of January 1. The roll opens for public inspection in May, which is when conferences and appeals happen, and bills are mailed in the fall. A 2 percent discount applies to payment by November 1, the face amount is due through December 31, and penalties of 5 percent in January and 10 percent after January 31 follow under KRS 134.015. Collection by the sheriff ends on April 15.

When bills run late, the state can approve a replacement calendar that gives one month per stage. A bill for omitted property, or for a value raised after an appeal, is due the day it is prepared.

sections.h2: What draws buyers to Bath County?
sections.html:
The county site promotes the outdoors: Cave Run Lake, a man made lake from the early 1970s popular for muskie fishing, and the Daniel Boone National Forest along its edge. The Owingsville and Bath County Chamber of Commerce describes Owingsville as the gateway to the Bluegrass on Interstate 64, and the Bath County Memorial Library sits on West Main Street.

History runs deep too. A 1932 archaeological field survey recorded fourteen sites in the county, including the Ramey Mound near Sharpsburg and burials near the Springfield Presbyterian Church. Sellers of rural land can ask the county clerk what is recorded against a tract before they list it.

The county sits in the Mount Sterling micropolitan area, which links to the Lexington region. Rural lots, small farms and homes near the lake and forest make up much of the market.

sections.h2: How is a Bath County assessment appealed?
sections.html:
Request a conference with the Bath County PVA while the roll is open in May. An agreed number ends the matter. Without one, you file at the clerk's office and name the value you claim.

Under KRS 133.030 a three member local board convenes at the county seat. Its first day goes to training and a review of recent comparable sales, and members may visit disputed properties. Five days is the ceiling unless the Department of Revenue permits more, and the decision arrives by certified mail.

  • Collect last year's sales of similar homes, photos of defects, and any appraisal.
  • Ask the PVA how recorded sales produced your value.
  • Add a repair estimate if a roof, well or septic problem is missing from the record.

The bill itself cannot be contested, since the filing window closed months before it arrived.

sections.h2: Which Bath County owners can claim the exemption?
sections.html:
A Bath County owner who reaches 65, or who is totally disabled, may claim it on the home where they live. File with the PVA in the year you want it and attach proof of age or disability.

Under KRS 132.810 each residential unit earns a single exemption, and a mobile home or manufactured house is treated as a unit, which suits a county where many owners live in one. The figure tracks the cost of living and is revisited every two years, so ask the PVA what applies. An owner approved after paying gets a refund for the exempt portion. A sale or a death goes on record with the PVA, and the buyer or heir files separately.

sections.h2: What becomes of unpaid Bath County taxes?
sections.html:
When April 15 passes, the sheriff hands any unpaid bill to the clerk, who files it as a delinquency certificate and lien. From then on interest accrues at 1 percent per month, and Revenue's worked examples stack commissions of 10 percent for the clerk and 20 percent for the county attorney on top.

Letters go out, parcels are advertised, and in summer a private buyer can purchase the certificate and add charges of its own. KRS 134.015 also makes the tax a personal debt of the January 1 owner and lets the lien trail the property for 11 years.

sections.h2: What should a rural Bath County seller know about land and forest?
sections.html:
Many parcels here include acreage. Working farmland is taxed at agricultural value instead of market value, a rule drawn from Section 172A of the state constitution, and buyers will want to know whether your acreage keeps the classification. Ask the PVA before you list.

Federal land is exempt from property tax, and a good part of the county lies inside the Daniel Boone National Forest, so check that a boundary on a rural tract matches both the recorded deed and the PVA map.

An older house with repairs pending and a bill sitting at the clerk's office can still sell. The payoff comes from the proceeds at closing, and the clerk quotes it for the month. A cash offer and a listing can be compared on what you net after repairs, back taxes and carrying costs.

faqs.q: Where do Bath County tax payments go?
faqs.a: Pay the Bath County Sheriff in Owingsville, whose office the county site lists at (606) 674-2931. Bills are mailed in the fall.

faqs.q: How long is the Bath County appeal window?
faqs.a: Only while the tax roll is open for inspection in May. Meet the PVA first, then file with the clerk on the next business day after the period closes.

faqs.q: How pricey is a Bath County home?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures give $129,800 for owned homes, with owners living in 74.7 percent of homes.

faqs.q: Does Bath County give a break to seniors?
faqs.a: Yes. An owner who is 65 or totally disabled can apply to the PVA under KRS 132.810 for the home they live in.

faqs.q: What follows once the clerk takes a Bath County bill?
faqs.a: Interest and fees are added, and the bill can be sold to a private buyer at a summer sale. Ask the clerk for a payoff and the county attorney about a payment plan.
